tagline.text: The Eastern Samar island where Magellan first set foot in 1521

location.label: Location
location.text: Homonhon Island, Guiuan, Eastern Samar (mouth of Leyte Gulf)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: A day trip or one night

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,500~4,000 (estimated boat and meals from Guiuan, per day)

children.text: This island belongs to Guiuan in Eastern Samar and is recorded as the place where Magellan's expedition first landed in the Philippines on March 16, 1521. It is a crescent-shaped island about 20 kilometers long, and a historical marker commemorating the landing stands there.

Homonhon is an island in the municipality of Guiuan, Eastern Samar, lying at the eastern mouth of Leyte Gulf. The coordinates given on English Wikipedia are 10°45′20″N, 125°44′21″E; the area is about 105.2 square kilometers and the coastline is about 57.5 kilometers. The island is about 20 kilometers long, and its highest point is Homonhon Peak at 374 meters above sea level. Wikipedia's nickname for it is Magellan's First Landing Site. A document on the protected area describes it as a crescent-shaped island covered in coconut trees.

The island has eight barangays: Bitaugan, Cagusu-an, Canawayon, Casuguran, Culasi, Habag, Inapulagan, and Pagbabangnan. By the 2020 census the barangays total 4,413 people, and the 2024 island population is given as 4,722. The largest settlement is Casuguran. It is a quiet, sparsely populated island, so do not expect large tourist facilities. The Guiuan protected landscape document names mangroves and seagrass beds as the main vegetation of the islands, and says a 2008 survey recorded the Philippine tarsier, the Philippine long-tailed macaque, the Philippine cockatoo, herons, egrets, terns, and monitor lizards; we could not confirm whether this record refers to Homonhon alone. Administratively, the island was part of Samar province until Republic Act No. 4221 split Samar into three provinces in 1965, and because it belongs to Guiuan it joined Eastern Samar. Just off the northwest tip of the island lies a small islet called Mantoconan.

Wikipedia says that on March 16, 1521 the three surviving ships of Magellan's expedition passed the Marianas and landed on this island. The island was uninhabited at the time, and two days later fishing boats from Suluan spotted the expedition. Local leaders arrived in more boats, welcomed the crew warmly, and traded food and supplies. The expedition rested for nearly two weeks, gathering fresh food and water, and left on March 27, and on March 28 it neared the island of Limasawa. The first Catholic Mass was held not on Homonhon but on Limasawa, on Easter Sunday, March 31. According to Wikipedia and the article on Suluan, the expedition dropped anchor here after crossing the Pacific in 98 days. The Suluan fishermen brought fish, palm liquor, bananas, and two coconuts, and the crew handed over trade goods, showed them the ship, and fired its mortars for them. On March 22 the fishermen came back with more coconuts, palm liquor, sweet oranges, and a rooster. The expedition had set out with five ships and about 270 men.

The island's story is not only about Western navigators. Wikipedia writes that, up to the early Spanish period, the Ibabaonon people of Samar's eastern coast regarded the island as the sacred home of Makapatag, the male aspect of the supreme diwata Malaon. On the other side, since the 1980s four large-scale nickel and chromite mining operations have been carried out on the island, and in April 2024 appeals were made to the National Historical Commission to save the island from mining. It helps to know that this is an island where history and environmental issues overlap.

According to Wikipedia, a historical marker stands on Homonhon commemorating Magellan's landing. We could not confirm its location or wording, so ask a local guide when you arrive. It is separate from the marker said to have been installed on Suluan in 2021 for the 500th anniversary.

After crossing the Pacific, Magellan led an expedition whose food had run out past the Marianas and reached this island. The crew rested here for nearly two weeks, gathering food and water, and left on March 27.
The island's highest point is Homonhon Peak at 374 meters above sea level. We could not confirm trail or guide information. If you want to climb it, consult a local guide.

blocks.title: A village island of eight barangays

children.text: The barangays are Bitaugan, Cagusu-an, Canawayon, Casuguran, Culasi, Habag, Inapulagan, and Pagbabangnan. The largest settlement is Casuguran.

The coastline reaches about 57.5 kilometers and the island is reportedly covered with coconut trees. It forms the northern boundary of the Surigao Strait at the mouth of Leyte Gulf. In World War II, on October 17, 1944, the US 6th Ranger Battalion landed on Dinagat, Homonhon, and Suluan and secured the entrance to Leyte Gulf, and MacArthur's Leyte landing followed three days later.

blocks.title: A sacred place of the Ibabaonon

children.text: Until the early Spanish period, the Ibabaonon people regarded this island as the sacred home of Makapatag. The island is both an early point of contact between East and West and a land of indigenous belief, which gives its story depth.

Four nickel and chromite mining operations have run since the 1980s, and appeals to protect the island were made again in 2024. The scenery and what you read may differ, so read the latest news before you visit.

Homonhon is included, along with Calicoan, Manicani, Suluan, Tubabao, and Victory, in the Guiuan Protected Landscape and Seascape. The area became a marine reserve under Proclamation No. 1801 on November 10, 1978, and was re-proclaimed under Proclamation No. 469 on September 26, 1994.
Ask for the Homonhon motorboat boarding point at Guiuan Transport Terminal. Confirm the village where you will land and your return boat at the same time.
Disembark in the village agreed when arranging the boat. Even if landing at Casuguran, check local transport and the distance to the Magellan landing marker separately.
In front of the marker, read the story of the March 16, 1521 landing and look around the nearby coast.
Have lunch in the village. There may be no restaurants, so it is safer to bring snacks and water.
Check the time of the last boat back first, and head to the pier without delay.
If the boat times are not certain, a day trip is risky. Plan to stay one night and check whether lodging is available.
Ask for the Homonhon motorboat boarding point at Guiuan Transport Terminal. Confirm the village where you will land and your return boat at the same time.
Walk through the village and look for the marker. If you have already confirmed that lodging is available, spend the time at sunset on the beach side.
If possible, look around the island's interior paths or coastline with a guide. We have no guidance information about climbing Homonhon Peak, so check locally.
Head to the pier in time for the boat back.
One night on the island means finding lodging and meals locally. Check whether you can book ahead and bring food.
A flight from Manila to Tacloban (TAC) is the most practical option.

We could not confirm local transport on the island. You may end up using motorcycles or walking.

Homonhon sits where the Pacific and Leyte Gulf meet, so sea conditions greatly decide whether you can travel. Choose a period of calm seas and check the marine forecast and whether boats are running before you leave.
A visit to the island may be possible all year, but boats can stop in typhoon season. We recommend planning with plenty of slack in case your schedule changes.
The expedition landed on March 16. We could not confirm whether any commemoration is held around that date, so ask the town hall first.

2019 Handig trip report

for a private boat one way. For current bookings, ask Guiuan Tourism about registered boats, capacity, life jackets and the return trip.

There is no hotel on the island; homestays or camping are common, and a guide mentions rooms and tents at Handig Beach, but no rates were found. One blog quotes about ₱100 for a public boat one way, but no official fare table was found. A traveler reported no grocery store at Handig Beach. Buy water and food for the return trip at the Guiuan public market or another store before sailing. Ask whether your lodging can provide meals.
Do not sail when a sea travel suspension is in force. Confirm the return boat before planning your day on the island.
Bring plenty of cash in pesos. It has not been confirmed that there is an ATM on the island.
Phone signal and electricity may be weak, so prepare a power bank and map files.
Pack water, snacks, a hat, and sunscreen.
It is safer to look for the Magellan landing marker with a guide.
Mining is a sensitive subject, so approach it carefully when talking with residents.
Because this is a marine protected area, do not step on or collect coral and seagrass. The area with the greatest variety of coral is described as the Suluan side.
We could not confirm scheduled boats or sailing times to the island. If a return boat is not guaranteed, avoid a day visit.
In typhoon season, boats can stop and the island can be isolated.
Entry fees, permits, and the availability of lodging must be confirmed locally first.
Medical facilities may be lacking, so bring basic medicines.
Mining activity and environmental issues on the island are ongoing, so the situation may change.

The island of the fishermen who first spotted the expedition in 1521. It has a cylindrical concrete lighthouse and is described as having 25 species of hard and soft corals. Check locally for how to get there.
The island the expedition neared on March 28 after leaving Homonhon, and the place known for the first Catholic Mass in the Philippines on Easter Sunday, March 31, 1521. The island is about
10km
long north to south, and its highest point is 848 meters above sea level. It is a different island from Homonhon, so if you want to include it, check locally how to get there.
